I think context is pretty important here. I'm a big believer that sexual objectification is fine - both genders do it. The issue arises if one is always sexually objectifying the opposite sex. For example, when making out on the sofa I'm probably not thinking about how much I respect her PhD and she's not thinking about how much she admires my photographic talents; when working together in a team at the office, responding in a sexual way is likely to make everyone in the team uncomfortable.

tl;dr - telling people not to objectify the opposite sex is dumb and counterproductive; teach them that it's only sometimes appropriate instead.

Thanks for the thoughtful response. May a propose a follow-up? There are people that are naturally attractive. They receive a disproportionate amount of sexual objectification because of this. What impact do you think this has on their day-to-day life?

There are various studies which show that attractive people are more successful - see, e.g, Daniel Hamermesh's work - but we're talking an earning difference of 3-4%. Day-to-day impact of this - probably not much.

The personal impact I think depends on when they realise they are "objectively" attractive (obviously in practice there is no single beauty consensus). If it happens when they are young then often it motivates lazy behaviour because they learn that they don't need try as hard. Conversely, those who realise it later often become insecure regarding any positive assessment from others, mistrusting whether it is genuine or because they are found attractive. Both of these are obviously massive generalisations that simply arise from my experience.

Fisher Price play people. They were perfect choking hazard size when I was growing up. I would play with those sets for hours, I had the town, the house and the farm. I would get them all set up and just play for days with them set up around my room. The new ones are huge and no fun, my kids weren't interested in the new fisher price at all. They did like the smaller (choking hazarding) play mobile, which I don't think existed when I was growing up. So in this case the new toys by a different company were better than the old company's new stuff. Does that make sense?

When I was a child we had great small vehicles; die cast trucks and realistic looking trains. Micro machines were awesome toys that could easily go with a child and be played with anywhere. Now all the trucks are plastic or not realistic, at least the ones I can find. All the trains have faces or anthropomorphic some how. I just want a non-wood diesel train and cars for my son to play with; and I have yet to find one.
